questions.prompt: A running process asks to read a file from the disk. Which state does it move to?
questions.explanation: A process that waits for input or output, or for any other event, is **waiting** (blocked). When the file has been read, it moves to **ready**, not straight back to running.

questions.prompt: A process arrives at 3 ms, needs 5 ms of CPU time and finishes at 14 ms. What is its waiting time, in ms?

Three processes are scheduled with **FCFS**: P1 arrives at 0 ms with a burst time of 6 ms, P2 at 1 ms with a burst of 2 ms, and P3 at 2 ms with a burst of 4 ms. Find the average waiting time in ms, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 0–6, P2 6–8, P3 8–12. The completion times are 6, 8 and 12, so the turnaround times are $6 - 0 = 6$, $8 - 1 = 7$ and $12 - 2 = 10$, and the waiting times are $6 - 6 = 0$, $7 - 2 = 5$ and $10 - 4 = 6$. Average WT $= \frac{0 + 5 + 6}{3} = \frac{11}{3} \approx 3.67$ ms.

questions.prompt: Four processes are scheduled with **SJF (non-preemptive)**. Arrival and burst times in ms: P1 (0, 8), P2 (1, 4), P3 (2, 9) and P4 (3, 2). Find the average turnaround time in ms.
questions.explanation: At 0 only P1 has arrived, so it runs 0–8. At 8, P2 (4), P3 (9) and P4 (2) are waiting: P4 is the shortest and runs 8–10, then P2 10–14, then P3 14–23. TAT: P1 $8 - 0 = 8$, P2 $14 - 1 = 13$, P3 $23 - 2 = 21$, P4 $10 - 3 = 7$. Average TAT $= \frac{8 + 13 + 21 + 7}{4} = \frac{49}{4} = 12.25$ ms.

questions.prompt: Three processes are scheduled with **Round Robin** and a time quantum of 3 ms. Arrival and burst times in ms: A (0, 5), B (1, 4) and C (4, 2). Find the average waiting time in ms, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: A runs 0–3 (2 ms left); B arrived at 1, so the queue is B, A. B runs 3–6 (1 ms left); C arrives at 4, so the queue is A, C, B. A runs 6–8 and finishes, C runs 8–10 and finishes, B runs 10–11 and finishes. $\text{WT} = \text{CT} - \text{AT} - \text{BT}$: A $8 - 0 - 5 = 3$, B $11 - 1 - 4 = 6$, C $10 - 4 - 2 = 4$. Average WT $= \frac{13}{3} \approx 4.33$ ms.

questions.prompt: In non-preemptive SJF, when a shorter process arrives, the running process is stopped so that the shorter one can run.
questions.explanation: Non-preemptive means a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or has to wait. The shorter process waits in the ready queue. (The preemptive version, Shortest Remaining Time First, is a different algorithm.)

questions.prompt: With FCFS, one long process at the front of the queue makes many short processes wait behind it. What is this problem called?
questions.explanation: This is the **convoy effect**. For bursts of 24, 3 and 3 ms arriving together, FCFS gives an average waiting time of 17 ms in the order 24, 3, 3, but only 3 ms in the order 3, 3, 24.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about Round Robin are true? Select **all** that apply.

choices.text: Each process runs for at most one time quantum before the next process gets the CPU
If the quantum is longer than every burst time, it works like FCFS
A very short quantum wastes CPU time on context switches
A long process can wait forever while short ones keep arriving

questions.explanation: Round Robin is preemptive: a process that has not finished after one quantum goes to the back of the queue. Every process in the queue gets a turn, so none waits forever. Starvation is a problem of SJF, not of Round Robin.

questions.prompt: With FCFS, P1 arrives at 0 ms with a burst time of 4 ms, and P2 arrives at 6 ms with a burst time of 3 ms. For how many ms is the CPU idle?
questions.explanation: P1 runs 0–4. No process is ready from 4 to 6, so the CPU is idle for $6 - 4 = 2$ ms. P2 then runs 6–9 with a waiting time of 0 ms. Show the idle time as a block in the Gantt chart.

questions.prompt: Three processes arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3, with burst times of 4, 6 and 3 ms. (a) Draw the Gantt chart for Round Robin with a time quantum of 3 ms. (b) Find the average waiting time. (c) FCFS gives an average waiting time of about 4.67 ms here. Give one reason why an operating system might still choose Round Robin.
questions.marking_guide: (a) 2 marks: P1 0–3, P2 3–6, P3 6–9, P1 9–10, P2 10–13, with the times under the edges of the boxes (1 mark for the order of the slices, 1 mark for the times). (b) 2 marks: waiting times P1 $10 - 4 = 6$, P2 $13 - 6 = 7$, P3 $9 - 3 = 6$ (1 mark), average $\frac{19}{3} \approx 6.33$ ms (1 mark). (c) 1 mark: Round Robin is fair and responds quickly, because every process gets the CPU within one round (here each starts within 6 ms), so no process waits behind a long one; this matters for interactive programs. Accept 'no starvation' or 'better response time'.
questions.explanation: (a) P1 0–3, P2 3–6, P3 6–9 (P3 finishes), P1 9–10 (finishes), P2 10–13 (finishes). (b) $\text{WT} = \text{CT} - \text{BT}$, because all arrive at 0: $10 - 4 = 6$, $13 - 6 = 7$ and $9 - 3 = 6$, so the average is $\frac{19}{3} \approx 6.33$ ms. (c) Round Robin gives every process the CPU quickly and fairly, which matters when people are using the computer.
